questions.stem: Which VIP condition makes upstream TLS available in this design?

choices.feedback: Correct: ssl-upstream is documented for server-type http on a server-load-balance VIP.
TCP virtual servers do not expose this HTTP upstream re-encryption option.
A static NAT VIP does not create the HTTP proxy transaction required here.
Proxy policies are not the VIP object that owns this upstream TLS setting.

questions.stem: Which observation proves encryption on the backend leg?

choices.feedback: An HTTP response proves service reachability, not backend transport protection.

choices.text: A capture shows TLS records upstream
choices.feedback: Correct: the upstream capture shows a TLS handshake and encrypted application records.

choices.text: The VIP appears in policy logs
choices.feedback: Policy logs prove policy processing, not the protocol used to the real server.

choices.text: The real server answers an ARP request
choices.feedback: ARP resolution proves Layer 2 reachability, not TLS session establishment.

questions.stem: What does ssl-http-strip-secure-cookies change in the response?

choices.feedback: The client-facing leg remains HTTP unless a separate HTTPS listener is used.
Certificate trust is controlled separately through backend verification and trust configuration.
Correct: the option removes Secure and related HTTPS-only Set-Cookie attributes for HTTP clients.
HTTP multiplexing is a separate connection-management feature.

questions.stem: What security property remains absent with upstream TLS enabled?

choices.feedback: Upstream TLS protects the FortiGate-to-realserver segment.

choices.text: The VIP selects a real server
choices.feedback: Real-server selection remains part of the load-balancing VIP function.

choices.text: The response is decrypted at FortiGate
choices.feedback: FortiGate must decrypt the backend response to proxy it to the client.
Correct: upstream TLS does not encrypt the client-facing HTTP segment.

questions.stem: Which setting is unsafe as a permanent backend-certificate workaround?

choices.feedback: Correct: disabling verification accepts untrusted or mismatched backend certificates.
A TLS minimum of 1.2 is a version-hardening control, not a trust bypass.
A trusted CA enables proper chain validation.
A client certificate is appropriate when the backend requests mutual TLS.

questions.stem: Which fields are central to disambiguating active user entries?

choices.feedback: Username and MAC alone do not show authentication method or virtual-domain context.
Correct: method, user group and VDOM are exposed by the monitor.
Policy and NAT data are not the monitor's documented identity dimensions.
Certificate details are not the fields described for this monitor.

questions.stem: What does Deauthenticate do to a selected firewall user?

choices.feedback: Session removal is not an identity lifecycle or account-disable operation.
Correct: the action deauthenticates the selected active session on its device context.
FortiManager does not delete the user from LDAP through this monitor.
No firewall deny policy is automatically created by deauthentication.

questions.stem: Two tenants use the same username on one managed firewall. What prevents confusion?

choices.feedback: A display name may be identical across virtual domains.
Group filtering narrows population but does not establish tenant context.
Policy revision is unrelated to the active session's VDOM identity.
Correct: VDOM distinguishes same-name entries in different virtual domains.

questions.stem: A user reappears immediately after deauthentication. What should be checked next?

choices.feedback: Correct: successful reauthentication indicates the account still matches an authentication rule and policy.
License state does not explain a user session that can authenticate again.
LLDP topology does not determine firewall user authentication.
ARP aging is unrelated to the identity reauthentication path.

questions.stem: Which prerequisites enable FortiMQ indicator delivery to FortiGate?

choices.feedback: FortiMQ is an alternative to FortiManager and does not require it.

choices.text: Same FortiCare account and feed sync
choices.feedback: Correct: same-account registration and Cloud-based Fabric Feed synchronization are required.
A local indicator alone does not establish cloud delivery or firewall retrieval.

choices.text: A syslog server and SNMP trap
choices.feedback: Syslog and SNMP do not replace the documented FortiMQ prerequisites.

questions.stem: What limits the scope of a FortiMQ block action?

choices.feedback: FortiMQ is not documented as a global all-device distribution mechanism.

choices.text: Every device in the FortiCare account
choices.feedback: FortiCare registration enables communication but does not define the block scope.

choices.text: FortiGate devices in the same ADOM
choices.feedback: Correct: indicators are applied to FortiGate devices in the same ADOM.
The connector distributes indicators to FortiGate external feeds, not only locally.

questions.stem: A connector reports healthy. What has actually been proven?

choices.feedback: Policy enforcement requires a separate matching deny-policy log.
Connector health does not prove downstream retrieval by every firewall.

choices.text: The indicator is in the right ADOM
choices.feedback: ADOM alignment is a separate scope check.
Correct: connector status reflects API connectivity to FortiMQ.

questions.stem: Both FortiMQ and FortiManager connectors are active. Which path has priority?

choices.feedback: Correct: FortiMQ is preferred; FortiManager is used if FortiMQ is disabled.
FortiManager remains supported but does not take priority in this condition.
Connector age is not the documented selection rule.

choices.text: The connector selected per firewall policy
choices.feedback: Firewall policy does not choose which connector transports indicators.

questions.stem: What does an sFlow packet sample represent?

choices.feedback: sFlow intentionally samples traffic and truncates packet information.
Correct: sampled flow records are statistical and may omit individual packets.
Session reconstruction is not guaranteed by sampled records.

choices.text: A mirrored copy of every frame
choices.feedback: Full-frame mirroring is a different mechanism from sFlow sampling.

questions.stem: What is the documented default sFlow collector UDP port?

choices.feedback: UDP 161 is commonly used for SNMP, not sFlow export.
UDP 514 is commonly used for syslog.
Correct: FortiSwitch sFlow collectors default to UDP 6343.
UDP 1812 is commonly used for RADIUS authentication.

questions.stem: Which command displays the switch's sFlow configuration?

choices.feedback: Correct: get system sflow displays the sFlow configuration.
PoE diagnostics show power state, not flow-export configuration.
IGMP snooping output describes multicast membership, not sFlow.
RADIUS user configuration is unrelated to flow sampling.

questions.stem: A collector IP responds to ping, but no flow data appears. What does ping prove?

choices.feedback: Sampler state must be inspected separately on each monitored interface.

choices.text: The collector decoded sFlow version five
choices.feedback: Collector decoding requires actual datagrams and supported format.

choices.text: The UDP collector port accepts packets
choices.feedback: Ping does not test UDP 6343 reachability.

choices.text: Only basic IP reachability is confirmed
choices.feedback: Correct: ping proves IP reachability only, not sFlow export or collection.

questions.stem: What is the documented default background rogue-AP scan cadence?

choices.text: Every 30 seconds, each scan lasts one second
choices.feedback: The guide documents a 300-second scan period, not a 30-second cycle.

choices.text: Every 300 seconds; each channel gets 20 ms
choices.feedback: Correct: each second a channel is monitored for 20 ms after a 300-second period begins.

choices.text: Only after an associated client disconnects
choices.feedback: Scanning is not triggered only by client disconnect events.

choices.text: Continuously while the radio serves clients
choices.feedback: Background scanning briefly switches the radio into monitor mode.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of ap-bgscan-idle?

choices.feedback: Transmit power is configured separately from scan scheduling.

choices.text: Change the rogue access point's MAC address
choices.feedback: Rogue AP identity is observed over the air and wired adjacency.

choices.text: Delay the next scan until radio idle
choices.feedback: Correct: the idle threshold reduces client packet loss during background scans.
The setting delays scanning; it does not disable WIDS detection.

questions.stem: Where is a WIDS profile applied for radio monitoring?

choices.text: On a radio through its FortiAP profile
choices.feedback: Correct: the WIDS profile is selected on a radio in a FortiAP profile.

choices.text: Inside a firewall address group object
choices.feedback: Firewall address groups do not configure wireless intrusion detection.

choices.text: Within a RADIUS user group definition
choices.feedback: RADIUS groups govern authentication, not radio scan behavior.
FortiAnalyzer receives logs but does not apply the AP radio profile.

questions.stem: No rogue AP entry appears in the dashboard. What can be concluded?

choices.text: The building has no unauthorized APs
choices.feedback: Absence of an entry is not proof that no AP exists.
Background scanning is periodic and channel-limited, not continuous.
An AP is not automatically accepted merely because no entry appears.

choices.text: Detection may be outside scan coverage
choices.feedback: Correct: range, channel coverage, scan timing and radio load affect visibility.

questions.stem: Which interface is explicitly unavailable for rogue-DHCP scanning?

choices.feedback: Correct: eth0 is reserved for management and cannot be used for this scan.
A dedicated interface is a documented implementation requirement.
The System DHCP Port represents the switch port carrying the scan NIC.
VLANs are selected for scanning; they are not the management interface.

questions.stem: How must an IP-helper address be represented for authorization?

choices.text: As a DNS alias without MAC
choices.feedback: A DNS alias does not provide the required IP/MAC identity pair.

choices.text: As a Pingable model with IP and MAC
choices.feedback: Correct: the helper address needs a Pingable model, MAC and authorized-group membership.

choices.text: As a firewall policy object only
choices.feedback: A firewall policy object is not the FortiNAC authorized DHCP inventory.

choices.text: As an unmodeled switch interface port
choices.feedback: Unmodeled infrastructure cannot satisfy the documented IP-helper comparison.

questions.stem: Which VLANs are included in a rogue-DHCP verification task?

choices.feedback: The task does not automatically scan every discovered VLAN.
Native VLAN status alone does not add a VLAN to the scan list.

choices.text: Only VLANs explicitly listed for scanning
choices.feedback: Correct: omitted VLANs are not scanned by this task.
eth0 is the management interface and cannot be the scan interface.

questions.stem: What must match across HA nodes for scanning to continue after failover?

choices.text: Only the scheduled task display name
choices.feedback: The task name does not establish the scan path on the secondary.

choices.text: Only the Authorized DHCP group label
choices.feedback: Group label alone does not ensure the scan NIC is attached correctly.
Administrator identity does not control the physical scan interface.

choices.text: The interface and System DHCP Port membership
choices.feedback: Correct: primary and secondary need matching interface and port-group configuration.

questions.stem: What must be true of an SNMPv3 trap sender?

choices.text: Modeled as a pingable Inventory device
choices.feedback: Correct: the trap sender must be modeled as a pingable device in Inventory.

choices.text: Configured only as an LDAP user object
choices.feedback: LDAP user records are not a substitute for sender modeling.

choices.text: Sending traps to UDP port 162 only
choices.feedback: The guide specifies FortiNAC trap reception on port 161.

choices.text: Absent from the FortiNAC Inventory view
choices.feedback: Unmodeled senders may not be accepted for record updates.

questions.stem: What is the effect of selecting SNMPv3 in the global SNMP settings?

choices.text: Only one trap sender's configuration changes
choices.feedback: The setting is global, not limited to one trap sender.

choices.text: All FortiNAC polling devices must use SNMPv3
choices.feedback: Correct: other devices querying FortiNAC must also use SNMPv3.

choices.text: SNMPv1 traps are automatically translated globally
choices.feedback: FortiNAC does not document automatic SNMP version translation.

choices.text: The management interface port number changes
choices.feedback: The SNMP setting does not change the management interface.

questions.stem: A user-removal trap arrives. What happens to associated hosts?

choices.feedback: User deletion does not automatically delete associated hosts.
FortiNAC documents the hosts becoming registered devices.
Correct: associated hosts remain and become registered devices.

choices.text: They are merged by MAC automatically
choices.feedback: Different adapters/MACs are treated as separate host records.

questions.stem: Which evidence confirms that FortiNAC processed a trap into a record change?

choices.feedback: Packet arrival proves transport, not parsing or database mutation.
Ping proves IP reachability only.
Configured credentials do not prove a trap was accepted.
Correct: the event plus resulting Host/User record confirms processing.

questions.stem: What ECDH curve preference is documented as the default for EAP?

choices.feedback: Correct: FortiAuthenticator documents secp521r1, secp384r1, then prime256v1.
The listed curves and ordering are not the documented default.
Those lower-strength curves are not the published default list.
That list is not the documented EAP ECDH preference.

questions.stem: What does the EAP ECDH override change?

choices.feedback: LDAP group membership is evaluated separately from TLS negotiation.
Correct: the command overrides ECDH_CURVE used for EAP TLS negotiation.
Certificate subject identity is not changed by the curve preference.
RADIUS shared-secret configuration is unrelated to ECDH curve selection.

questions.stem: What distinguishes EAP-TLS from a one-way server-authenticated tunnel?

choices.feedback: EAP-TLS relies on certificates rather than removing validation.
TLS is central to EAP-TLS.
Correct: EAP-TLS authenticates both client and server with certificates.
RADIUS policy still controls whether the authenticated identity is authorized.

questions.stem: Which EAP-TTLS 2FA limitation is documented?

choices.text: EAP-TTLS supports interactive challenge-based token prompts
choices.feedback: The guide explicitly states challenge-based EAP-TTLS 2FA is unsupported.

choices.text: EAP-TTLS bypasses its inner password method
choices.feedback: EAP-TTLS does not skip its inner authentication method.

choices.text: Only SMS second factors are supported here
choices.feedback: SMS is not the documented required method for this limitation.
Correct: use password-plus-OTP concatenation for EAP-TTLS with 2FA.

questions.stem: What is the default state of require-message-authenticator?

choices.text: Enabled by default on each server
choices.feedback: Correct: FortiPAM enables response Message-Authenticator validation by default.

choices.text: Disabled by default on each server
choices.feedback: The option is not disabled by default.

choices.text: Inherited from the selected user group
choices.feedback: The setting is under the RADIUS server object, not user group.

choices.text: Enabled only for TLS transport sessions
choices.feedback: The documented default is enabled, not conditional on TLS.

questions.stem: Which RADIUS attribute carries the Message-Authenticator?

choices.feedback: Attribute 26 is Vendor-Specific, not Message-Authenticator.
Correct: Message-Authenticator is RADIUS Attribute 80.
Attribute 44 is Acct-Session-Id.
Attribute 61 is NAS-Port-Type.

questions.stem: When is disabling response validation acceptable?

choices.feedback: A single failed test needs diagnosis, not automatic weakening.
Global weakening increases exposure beyond the affected server.

choices.text: As a scoped temporary compatibility fallback
choices.feedback: Correct: disable only temporarily for a server that cannot return the attribute.
Message-Authenticator does not replace shared-secret correctness.

questions.stem: A response has Attribute 80 but validation fails. What should be checked?

choices.feedback: User role is evaluated after successful RADIUS authentication.

choices.text: Only the target server's DNS record
choices.feedback: DNS resolution alone cannot explain an invalid response authenticator.
Wireless radio configuration is unrelated to RADIUS integrity.

choices.text: Shared secret and response HMAC calculation
choices.feedback: Correct: verify the shared secret and the server's Attribute 80 calculation.

questions.stem: Which evaluation mode is designed for real-time in-memory processing?

choices.feedback: Correct: Streaming evaluates incoming events in memory in real time.
Scheduled mode uses disk and configured query windows.
Scheduled via SQL executes scheduled SQL against ClickHouse.
Archive rebuild is not a rule evaluation mode.

questions.stem: Where is Scheduled via SQL available?

choices.feedback: The guide restricts this mode to ClickHouse.
Correct: Scheduled via SQL is visible only in Super/Global mode on ClickHouse.
Collector-node placement is not the documented availability condition.
Scheduled via SQL is distinct from Streaming mode.

questions.stem: Which limitation is specific to Scheduled via SQL?

choices.feedback: The guide states Scheduled via SQL incidents do not show trigger events.

choices.text: It can be tested like Streaming
choices.feedback: Scheduled via SQL cannot be tested like a Streaming rule.

choices.text: No trigger events; 100 incidents per run
choices.feedback: Correct: it has no trigger events and caps each run at 100 incidents.

choices.text: Clear conditions can use any field
choices.feedback: Only time is supported as a clear condition.

questions.stem: Why might Scheduled mode be chosen over Streaming?

choices.text: It always provides lower detection latency
choices.feedback: Streaming is designed for lower-latency event processing.
Scheduled mode requires disk access.

choices.text: It guarantees every event is processed immediately
choices.feedback: Scheduled evaluation runs on a configured schedule, not instantly.

choices.text: It supports larger windows and complex analytics
choices.feedback: Correct: scheduled rules can use complex analytic functions over larger windows.

questions.stem: What FortiClient baseline enables IP range/CIDR ZTNA destinations?

choices.feedback: Correct: the feature is supported for FortiClient for Windows 7.2.8 or later.
The documented prerequisite is specifically Windows FortiClient 7.2.8+.
Version 6.4 does not meet the stated requirement.
Agent-based ZTNA uses the FortiClient endpoint.

questions.stem: What activates a private application for an endpoint?

choices.text: Creating only the application gateway object
choices.feedback: A gateway alone is only the entry point.

choices.text: Referencing it in an endpoint-profile connection rule
choices.feedback: Correct: the endpoint profile must reference the private application in a ZTNA rule.

choices.text: Adding it to a FortiAnalyzer report view
choices.feedback: FortiAnalyzer reports do not provision endpoint ZTNA destinations.

choices.text: Changing the client's DNS suffix setting
choices.feedback: DNS suffix changes do not bind the application to a profile.

questions.stem: What does the ZTNA profile Encryption toggle protect?

choices.feedback: The toggle is a traffic transport option, not database encryption.
SAML signing is separate from the tunnel encryption setting.

choices.text: Traffic between FortiClient and the application gateway
choices.feedback: Correct: it controls encryption between the endpoint and the gateway.
Backend disk encryption is unrelated to this endpoint-profile option.

questions.stem: A catalogue object exists but the endpoint cannot connect. What is the next check?

choices.text: Assume the gateway policy is already correct
choices.feedback: Object creation alone does not prove endpoint assignment or authorization.

choices.text: Delete every private application object from profile
choices.feedback: Deleting every object removes useful configuration evidence.

choices.text: Change the FortiSASE client IP pool range
choices.feedback: IP pool settings do not fix a missing ZTNA rule binding.

choices.text: Verify profile binding, client version and gateway reachability
choices.feedback: Correct: verify client support, endpoint profile reference and gateway reachability.

questions.stem: What is the hybrid strategy's first ranking criterion?

choices.feedback: Correct: members with the highest SLA value are selected first.
Quality is considered only after SLA value and cost tie.
Cost is the first tie-breaker, not the initial ranking criterion.
Configuration order is the final tie-breaker.

choices.feedback: Latency is considered after SLA value and cost remain tied.
Correct: administrative cost is the first tie-breaker after SLA value.
Interface index is not the documented ranking stage.
BGP router ID is not part of this service-rule algorithm.

questions.stem: What does custom-profile-1 combine?

choices.text: Only the physical interface speed value
choices.feedback: Interface speed alone is not the custom profile formula.
Packet loss can be one weighted component but is not the only one.

choices.text: Weighted loss, latency, jitter and reciprocal bandwidth
choices.feedback: Correct: the custom profile can weight four link-quality measurements.

choices.text: Only the advertised BGP MED metric
choices.feedback: BGP MED is separate from the SD-WAN health-check custom profile.

questions.stem: Which command output shows the service-rule member ranking and selection?

choices.feedback: Health-check output shows measurements and SLA state, not full rule ranking.
BGP summary shows neighbor state, not SD-WAN service selection.
NIC hardware counters do not show service-rule ranking.
Correct: service4 shows tie-break mode, member order, SLA and selected interface.

questions.stem: What does link-cost-threshold control in the hybrid rule?

choices.text: The number of members in a zone
choices.feedback: minimum-sla-meet-members controls zone eligibility, not this threshold.
custom-profile-threshold determines whether the custom SLA passes.

choices.text: Percentage change that triggers route regeneration
choices.feedback: Correct: link-cost-threshold controls percentage change before policy-route regeneration.
BGP neighbor count is unrelated to link-cost route regeneration.
